Below are the project objectives as listed in the Statement of Project Objectives (SOPO): 1. Detailed process models for chemical and solvent-based upcycling of waste plastics. 2. Collection, sorting technology, and practice that improve the volume, composition, and quality of baled plastics from Material Recovery Facilities (MRFs). 3. Production of plastic-derived oils from thermal depolymerization of mixed plastic waste streams in laboratory and pilot plant scale. 4. Catalytic upgrading of plastic-derived oils into aromatics and olefins (plastic monomers) in a continuous flow reactor. 5. Use of solvent-based recycling strategies for converting multi-layer films into pure resins. 6. Development of undergraduate and graduate curriculum material for plastic recycling CUWP was selected from DE-FOA-0002203 FY20 Multi-Topic FOA, Topic Area 6b: Waste Plastics to Products, that required collaboration with at least one university in both Canada and Mexico to leverage capacity and capitalize on North American resources. The full partners for this project are shown in Section 7. Professors from both Mexico and Canada participated in CUWP for the entire research program. CUWP funded travel for Canada and Mexico, professors and their students to attend CUWP meetings and do research stays at CUWP institutions. Industrial partners from Canada, Mexico and South America joined the CUWP industrial advisory board and participated with CUWP research activities. 3. Project Results and Discussion Topic Area 1 – Systems Analysis of Chemical Recycling Plastic Infrastructure Under Task 2.1, we developed a robust framework to benchmark and screen plastic recycling and upcycling technologies using techno-economic analysis (TEA), life-cycle assessment (LCA), supply chain modeling, and machine learning. In Subtask 2.1.1, we first developed consistent economic and environmental baselines across solvent-based recycling, thermochemical upcycling, and material recovery systems. These benchmarks were then used within process modeling studies as part of Subtask 2.1.2. We have used our methods for analyzing a broad variety of recycling/upcycling pathways studied in the CUWP project (e.g., STRAP variants, hydroformylation, catalytic upgrading, pyrolysis, and thermal oxo degradation) (Li et al., 2023a; Ma et al., 2023; Olafasakin, Ma, Zavala, et al., 2023; Sánchez Rivera et al., 2021). In the case of solvent-based recycling technologies, prior models have shown this method to be economic unreasonable due to the high costs of solve‐nt distillation. Distillation would be required in the case of using anti-solvents which prior to our work is considered state of the art. In Sanchez et al. we evaluated and compared various configurations for our solvent targeted recovery and precipitation (STRAP) process upcycling of post-industrial waste(Sánchez Rivera et al., 2021). The results demonstrate that this process can also recover polymers at similar costs to those of virgin resins, indicating that the STRAP technology is fle‐xible and can remain economically competitive as the plastic feed complexity is increased. The work reported in Munguía-López et al. quantified carbon footprint, energy use, and water consumption for multiple STRAP process configurations (Munguía-López et al., 2023b).
